 Search Icon Search Icon (Image: ViaJiin) A beginner's guide to Korean skincare, with glowing advice from a Renton insider
 Kate Neidigh November 11, 2026 19 View all photos Lately, people have been asking what I’m doing to my skin. This is a question I’m very happy to answer.
 Apparently, I have a glow. As a working mom of two who would generally settle for looking well-rested, I’ll take it.
 About a month ago, I took a skin quiz through Renton-based ViaJiin and committed to the Korean skincare routine founder Agnes Kim recommended for me. I wanted more hydration, smoother-looking skin and someone to explain what an ampoule actually does.
 A full month in, I swear I’m never looking back. But before we get to my bathroom cabinet, let’s clear up the biggest thing that kept me from exploring Korean beauty sooner: I thought it sounded like a lot of work.
 Turns out, the famous 10-step routine isn’t a requirement. Kim says that idea made Korean skincare sound far more time-consuming than it needs to be.
 “Most people I know in Korea do four or five steps, and many do fewer,” she says.
 Excellent. I have enough jobs.
 Your Korean beauty friend, right here in Renton
 Kim was born in the U.S. and lived in Korea from ages 8 to 15. Growing up, skincare was an ordinary part of the day. She remembers trying one of her mom’s toners and being delighted by how it felt.
 “My mom never wore much makeup, and to this day she isn’t great at it, but she always had her basic skincare covered,” she says.
 Kim went on to work at Sony Pictures Entertainment and Microsoft’s Xbox business, while becoming the person friends turned to for Korean skincare recommendations.
 She started building ViaJiin on nights and weekends in late 2025. When her Microsoft role was eliminated this summer, she went all in.
 “Jiin” means someone you know in Korean, which gets at the idea behind the business.
 “That’s what I want to be for people: your insider to Korean beauty.”
 Kim sources products directly from Korea, talks with founders and chemists, reviews ingredient lists and digs into Korean customer reviews. She pays particular attention to reviews from people who purchased products with their own money.
 For anyone who has ever wondered whether a glowing product review came with a paycheck, that detail is appreciated.
 You can start small. Really.
 Kim describes Korean beauty as consistent, gentle skincare with an emphasis on hydration. And you don’t need an entire shelf to get started.
 Her three essentials are cleanser, moisturizer and sunscreen. From there, a hydrating toner can add moisture, and a serum or ampoule can address a particular concern.
 For mornings, she suggests a gentle cleanse, hydrating toner, moisturizer and sunscreen. At night, cleanse away sunscreen and the day’s buildup, then follow with toner, an optional treatment and cream.
 “Masks, essences, eye creams and exfoliants are nice to have, not need to have,” she says.
 That sheet mask you’ve been saving for a quiet evening? Enjoy it when the opportunity presents itself. You haven’t failed skincare if that evening takes a while to arrive.
 Wait, what’s an ampoule?
 I needed this explained, too. Here’s Kim’s guide to a few words you’ll encounter while browsing:
 Toner: A watery step after cleansing. Kim favors hydrating formulas, a welcome departure from the sting-your-face toners some of us grew up using.
 Essence: A lightweight layer focused mostly on hydration, often slightly thicker than toner.
 Serum: A treatment formulated for a particular goal, such as a brighter or firmer appearance.
 Ampoule: Another treatment format, often marketed as more concentrated. Kim says the distinction between a serum and an ampoule depends on the brand.
 Do you need all four? You do not. Kim generally recommends a toner and one treatment step for people ready to add to the basics.
 A word for my fellow enthusiastic exfoliators
 I went into this conversation with questions about clogged pores and uneven texture. I also admitted that I exfoliate once or twice a week, despite occasionally being told during facials to ease up.
 Kim had some thoughts.
 “The most common mistake is over-exfoliating,” she says. “People want glow, so they scrub and peel more.”
 She describes the skin barrier as a brick wall, with skin cells as the bricks and lipids, including ceramides, helping form the mortar that holds moisture in. Her approach is to get skin feeling comfortable before adding more intensive treatments.
 It also means taking your time with new products. Tempting as it is to unpack everything and immediately have a full spa evening, Kim recommends introducing products gradually so you can tell what agrees with your skin.
 She also points out that persistent redness, visible blood vessels or unexplained changes are reasons to check in with a dermatologist.
 “A good routine supports your skin,” she says. “It doesn’t replace a doctor.”
 What ended up in my bathroom cabinet
 My skin quiz initially matched me with ViaJiin’s Lift & Renewal Kit. Then Kim read my follow-up answers about exfoliation and sensitivity and changed her recommendation to Restore & Nourish .
 I liked that she reconsidered. Those extra questions about my existing products, preferences and past reactions actually informed what she chose.
 I told her I love a rich cream, want to look a little less tired and have had breakouts with certain facial oils. She recommended a Dr.RELIEF cleanser and toner, followed by Healara’s Core Lift Firming Ampoule and Core Revive Activating Cream. She highlighted ceramides, peptides and the rich, fragrance-free cream as reasons for the selection.
 She also added the Vegetology Viniferine Ampoule , a separate treatment focused on a more even-looking complexion.
 ViaJiin provided the products for me to try, and I gave the suggested routine a full month. Once I learned the order, it was easy to work into my mornings and evenings. And then came the questions from friends about my skin.
 Apparently, the glow had entered the chat.
 That’s my personal experience, and everyone’s skin is different. But having someone help me choose a routine made me much more inclined to stick with it. I knew what each bottle was doing there, which was a considerable improvement over my previous shopping strategy of “this sounds promising.”
 A few things to remember when shopping
 For Seattle’s cooler months, Kim suggests adjusting moisture levels as needed, perhaps with a richer night cream, and going easier on exfoliation. Sunscreen stays in the morning routine, cloudy skies included.
 If you’re watching your budget, she recommends putting more toward your moisturizer and, if you want one, a targeted treatment. Cleanser can be a place to save. You can also skip collecting multiple exfoliants.
 Her most useful shopping advice might be this:
 “Everyone else calling something the best product ever doesn’t mean it’s the best product for you.”
 Fair. I’ve bought enough products on the strength of a stranger’s excellent lighting.
 For now, I’m sticking with the bottles Kim picked for me. A month of consistency, a routine I actually enjoy and unsolicited skin compliments? I’m making room on the counter.
